facts.finding: In a study of chess players, the strongest predictor of chess skill was the amount of serious study done alone, more than the amount of tournament play.
facts.source_text: Charness et al., Applied Cognitive Psychology, 2005

facts.finding: Shown a real game position for five seconds, chess masters rebuilt almost all of it from memory while beginners placed only a few pieces. With randomly scrambled pieces the masters' advantage almost disappeared: they remember patterns, not single pieces.
Fifth graders praised for being smart later avoided harder problems and did worse after a setback; children praised for their effort chose harder problems and kept trying.
facts.source_text: Mueller & Dweck, J. Pers. Soc. Psychol., 1998

facts.finding: Students who tested themselves on material remembered much more of it a week later than students who simply studied it again, even though re-studying felt more effective.
A review of hundreds of learning experiments found that the same amount of practice is remembered far longer when it is spread over several sessions instead of done all at once.
Among chess players who reached master level, the amount of practice it took varied enormously: some got there in about three thousand hours, others needed more than twenty thousand.

In a study of violin students at a music academy, the best players had spent far more hours practising alone than the less accomplished ones, and they rated practice alone as the activity that mattered most for improving.

People learned to recognise painters' styles better when paintings by different artists were mixed together than when they were grouped by artist, even though most of them believed grouping had worked better.

Students who practised different kinds of maths problems mixed together scored far higher on a test a week later than students who practised one kind at a time, although practising one kind at a time felt easier.

Among finalists of the National Spelling Bee, the hours spent studying words alone predicted how far they got better than being quizzed by others or reading for pleasure, and the children rated that solitary study as the hardest and least enjoyable activity.
facts.source_text: Duckworth et al., Social Psychological and Personality Science, 2011

facts.finding: In a study of young chess players, the amount of practice predicted chess skill better than intelligence did.

When grandmasters and strong club players thought aloud about the same position, the grandmasters did not calculate more moves or look further ahead: they simply considered better moves from the start.
facts.source_text: de Groot, Thought and Choice in Chess, 1965
